text.title: Glossary Management as Code Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for glossary-management-as-code. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Glossary MUST live in a single `glossary.yaml` (or split by domain) in the repo root; markdown / wiki copies are derived artefacts only.
rule.rationale: Terminology has authority only when there is exactly one place it can be wrong. With a wiki page, a spec and a slide deck each carrying definitions, they diverge silently and every reader believes their copy is current. Keeping the source structured, in-repo and machine-readable also means derived copies are generated rather than retyped, and retyping is where the drift starts.

rule.statement: Each term MUST carry: canonical_form, definition, synonyms[], deprecated_aliases[], owner, last_reviewed, related[].
rule.rationale: A definition on its own does not settle the argument a glossary exists to end, which is whether two words denote the same thing. Synonyms and deprecated aliases let a reader who arrives with the wrong word land on the right entry; owner and last_reviewed let a reader judge whether to trust it; related links expose the case where two entries quietly overlap.

rule.statement: Every glossary change MUST go through a PR; the PR description MUST cite the trigger (new feature, audit finding, term collision).
rule.rationale: A definition change is a silent behaviour change, because it retroactively alters what every existing requirement, ticket and test using that term meant. Review puts it in front of the people holding those artefacts before it lands. Requiring the trigger in the description is what makes the history usable: a diff shows what changed, only the trigger shows whether it was a real domain shift or one person's preference.

rule.statement: Each term MUST have a single named owner — never 'the team'; un-owned terms auto-flag for cleanup quarterly.
rule.rationale: A term owned by the team is owned by nobody: when two readings collide there is no one whose call settles it, so the collision gets resolved differently in each implementation. A named owner also gives the staleness sweep a destination, without which the auto-flag just produces a queue nobody is accountable for draining.

rule.statement: Each term carries a last_reviewed ISO date; terms not reviewed in 6 months are auto-flagged stale and routed to the owner.
rule.rationale: Definitions rot invisibly. The product moves, the wording stays, and readers keep trusting it because a glossary carries no signal of age. A dated review turns silence into evidence: a term untouched for six months is either genuinely stable, which costs a minute to confirm, or abandoned, and the flag is the only thing that distinguishes the two.

rule.statement: Removed terms are moved to deprecated_aliases of their replacement; outright deletion is forbidden so old artefacts remain interpretable.
rule.rationale: Deleting a term does not delete the thousands of tickets, specs and commit messages that used it; it only removes the one place that explained what they meant. A reader of a two-year-old requirement is then left with an unresolvable word. Keeping the old form as an alias of its replacement preserves the mapping, so historical artefacts stay readable and searches on the old term still land.

rule.statement: If term A names B as synonym, B's record MUST name A as synonym; asymmetric synonym links are auto-flagged.
rule.rationale: Synonymy is symmetric in the domain but not in the file, because whoever adds the link edits only the record they happened to be looking at. The result resolves when you enter by one term and fails when you enter by the other, and the reader who hits the failing direction concludes the two terms denote different things, which is the exact confusion the glossary was built to prevent.

rule.statement: If the project has no recurring vocabulary drift or no PR culture, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: The overhead here, PRs plus owners plus review dates plus symmetry checks, is paid per change and repays itself only through repeated cross-party misunderstandings avoided. A single author has no counterparty to misunderstand, and a freely edited wiki cannot enforce any of the rules, so adopting the shape without the review gate buys the ceremony and none of the control.
